title: Beat the money in one primary and it just shows up in the next one
body: Last week in Michigan, money hit a wall. The Lever reports Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic Senate primary over establishment pick Haley Stevens in what was likely the most expensive Democratic primary in US history. On election night El-Sayed told supporters the super PACs outspent him 11 to 1 and spent $70 million trying to stop him. He won anyway. It looked like a turning point.

Then look at Minnesota. Drop Site reports that four super PACs tied to AIPAC and Democratic Majority for Israel poured more than $3 million into a quiet House primary to replace Angie Craig, and the vote is today. The play is not just to fund their preferred candidate, state senator Matt Klein. It is to split the opposition. Pro-Israel money lifts Klein while other PACs quietly boost a second progressive, Kaela Berg, to pull votes from the frontrunner, Matt Little. One group alone, 314 Action, spent about $2.5 million backing Klein in a race that used to be sleepy.

That is the real lesson of this cycle. The money does not need to win every race. It just needs to keep showing up, in smaller contests, later in the calendar, through PACs with clean-sounding names. El-Sayed proved it can be beaten. Minnesota shows how much it costs to beat it, every single time.
